_link.title: I can explain retrieval and how information moves from LTM back to STM

toLevel2.stem: What is retrieval in the context of the Atkinson-Shiffrin model?

options.text: The process of accessing information stored in LTM and bringing it into conscious awareness in STM
options.explanation: Retrieval is the process of accessing information stored in LTM and bringing it into conscious awareness in STM, triggered by retrieval cues.

options.text: The process of transferring information from sensory memory directly into long-term memory
options.explanation: This describes encoding from sensory memory, not retrieval. Retrieval moves information from LTM back to STM.

options.text: The process of permanently deleting information that is no longer needed from memory
options.explanation: Retrieval does not delete information. It accesses stored information in LTM and brings it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: The process of holding new sensory information in short-term memory for immediate use
options.explanation: This describes the initial holding of information in STM, not retrieval. Retrieval specifically moves information from LTM back to STM.

toLevel2.stem: In the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, retrieval moves information in which direction?

options.text: From LTM back to STM
options.explanation: Retrieval moves information from long-term memory back into short-term memory, where it becomes consciously available.

options.text: From STM forward to LTM
options.explanation: Moving information from STM to LTM is encoding, not retrieval. Retrieval moves information in the opposite direction.

options.text: From sensory memory to STM
options.explanation: Moving information from sensory memory to STM is part of initial encoding, not retrieval from LTM.

options.text: From STM back to sensory memory
options.explanation: Information does not move from STM back to sensory memory. Retrieval moves information from LTM to STM.

toLevel2.stem: What triggers the retrieval of information from long-term memory?

options.text: Retrieval cues
options.explanation: Retrieval is triggered by retrieval cues — stimuli or prompts that activate the stored information in LTM and bring it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: Sensory overload
options.explanation: Sensory overload does not trigger retrieval. Retrieval is triggered by retrieval cues that activate stored information.

options.text: Memory displacement
options.explanation: Displacement is a cause of forgetting in STM, not a trigger for retrieval from LTM.

options.text: Information decay
options.explanation: Decay is a cause of forgetting, not a trigger for retrieval. Retrieval is triggered by retrieval cues.

toLevel2.stem: When retrieved information enters STM, what does the person become?

options.text: Consciously aware of the information
options.explanation: Retrieval brings information from LTM into conscious awareness in STM, making it available for current use.

options.text: Unable to process any new information
options.explanation: Retrieval does not prevent processing of new information. It brings stored information into conscious awareness.

options.text: Permanently unable to forget the retrieved information
options.explanation: Retrieved information in STM is still subject to STM's limited duration and can be forgotten again.

options.text: Unconsciously conditioned to avoid the information
options.explanation: Retrieval brings information into conscious awareness, not unconscious conditioning.

toLevel2.stem: A student reads the keyword 'hippocampus' and this brings related information about its role in explicit memory into conscious awareness. What is the keyword acting as?

options.text: A retrieval cue
options.explanation: The keyword 'hippocampus' acts as a retrieval cue, triggering the retrieval of related information from LTM into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: A sensory register
options.explanation: A sensory register holds brief sensory impressions. The keyword functions as a retrieval cue that activates stored information in LTM.

options.text: A displacement trigger
options.explanation: Displacement pushes information out of STM. The keyword functions as a retrieval cue, not a displacement trigger.

options.text: An encoding barrier
options.explanation: An encoding barrier would prevent information from being stored. The keyword functions as a retrieval cue that activates stored information.

toLevel2.stem: Retrieval is the process of accessing information stored in LTM and bringing it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: True
options.explanation: This is the correct definition of retrieval. It moves information from LTM back into STM where it becomes consciously available.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Retrieval does access information in LTM and bring it into conscious awareness in STM.

toLevel2.stem: Retrieval is triggered by retrieval cues that activate information stored in long-term memory.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Retrieval cues are stimuli or prompts that trigger the retrieval process, activating stored information in LTM and bringing it into STM.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is true. Retrieval is indeed triggered by retrieval cues that activate stored information in LTM.

toLevel2.stem: Retrieval is the process of accessing information stored in {{blank:1}} and bringing it into conscious awareness in {{blank:2}}.
Retrieval is triggered by retrieval {{blank:1}} that activate stored information and bring it into {{blank:2}} awareness.
When a student reads the keyword 'hippocampus', it acts as a {{blank:1}} cue, bringing related information from {{blank:2}} into STM.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best explains why some memories feel inaccessible even though they are stored in LTM?

options.text: The right retrieval cue may not have been encountered to trigger the retrieval process
options.explanation: Retrieval requires appropriate cues. If the right cue has not been encountered, the information remains in LTM but cannot be brought into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: The information has been permanently deleted from LTM and can never be recovered
options.explanation: Information in LTM is not necessarily permanently deleted. It may be inaccessible because the right retrieval cue has not been encountered.

options.text: STM has reached its maximum capacity and cannot accept any further information from LTM
options.explanation: While STM has limited capacity, the primary reason memories feel inaccessible is the absence of appropriate retrieval cues, not STM being full.

options.text: Sensory memory is blocking the transfer of information from LTM back into short-term memory
options.explanation: Sensory memory does not block retrieval from LTM. Inaccessibility occurs when the right retrieval cue has not been encountered.

toLevel3.stem: How does retrieval explain the way past learning becomes available for current use?

options.text: Retrieval cues activate stored information in LTM, bringing it into STM where it can be consciously used
options.explanation: Retrieval explains how past learning becomes available by showing that cues activate stored LTM information and bring it into conscious awareness in STM for current use.

options.text: Past learning is always consciously available without any need for retrieval cues or processes
options.explanation: Past learning is not always consciously available. It must be retrieved from LTM into STM through retrieval cues.

options.text: Past learning is permanently held in STM so it is always immediately available without retrieval
options.explanation: STM has limited duration and capacity. Past learning is stored in LTM and must be retrieved into STM to be used.

options.text: Retrieval permanently moves information out of LTM so it can only be used once before it is lost
options.explanation: Retrieval does not remove information from LTM. It copies information into STM while the original remains stored in LTM.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes retrieval from encoding in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model?

options.text: Encoding transfers information from STM to LTM, while retrieval transfers it from LTM back to STM
options.explanation: Encoding moves information into LTM for storage, while retrieval accesses that stored information and brings it back into STM for conscious use.

options.text: Both encoding and retrieval move information in the same direction from sensory memory to LTM
options.explanation: Encoding and retrieval move information in opposite directions. Encoding goes toward LTM; retrieval comes back from LTM to STM.

options.text: Encoding requires retrieval cues while retrieval requires rehearsal to move information between stores
options.explanation: This reverses the mechanisms. Retrieval requires cues, while encoding is supported by rehearsal and elaboration.

options.text: Encoding and retrieval are identical processes that occur simultaneously in sensory memory only
options.explanation: Encoding and retrieval are distinct processes moving information in opposite directions between STM and LTM.

toLevel3.stem: Why is retrieval considered essential in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model, rather than being an optional process?

options.text: Without retrieval, information in LTM cannot enter conscious awareness and is unavailable for use
options.explanation: Retrieval is essential because stored information in LTM must be brought into STM to be consciously used. Without retrieval, LTM information remains inaccessible.

options.text: Retrieval is optional because all information in LTM is permanently and automatically available to conscious awareness
options.explanation: LTM information is not automatically available. Retrieval is the necessary process that brings it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: Retrieval is optional because sensory memory can directly access LTM without involving STM at all
options.explanation: Sensory memory does not directly access LTM. Retrieval from LTM into STM is necessary for conscious use of stored information.

options.text: Retrieval is only needed for information stored in sensory memory, not information in long-term memory
options.explanation: Retrieval specifically refers to accessing information in LTM and bringing it into STM. It is not about sensory memory.

toLevel3.stem: Which of the following best explains the role of retrieval cues in the memory process?

options.text: They act as triggers that activate specific information stored in LTM, initiating the retrieval process
options.explanation: Retrieval cues are stimuli that activate specific stored information in LTM, triggering its transfer into STM for conscious awareness.

options.text: They permanently erase information from LTM once the information has been brought into STM
options.explanation: Retrieval cues do not erase information. They activate stored information so it can be brought into conscious awareness.

options.text: They block the transfer of information from sensory memory to STM during the encoding process
options.explanation: Retrieval cues facilitate access to LTM, not block encoding. They are triggers for the retrieval process.

options.text: They increase the physical capacity of STM to hold more items during the retrieval process itself
options.explanation: Retrieval cues do not increase STM capacity. They activate stored LTM information, triggering its transfer to STM.

toLevel3.stem: A student studies a topic thoroughly but cannot recall any information during an exam. After the exam, a classmate mentions a keyword from the topic and the student immediately recalls the material. Which concept does this best illustrate?

options.text: The keyword acted as a retrieval cue that activated the stored information in LTM
options.explanation: The keyword served as a retrieval cue, activating the stored information in LTM and bringing it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: The information was never encoded into LTM and was created from the keyword alone
options.explanation: The student studied thoroughly, indicating the information was in LTM. The keyword triggered retrieval of existing stored information.

options.text: The classmate's keyword permanently restored information that had been deleted from LTM
options.explanation: The information was not deleted. It was in LTM but inaccessible until the right retrieval cue was encountered.

options.text: The student's sensory memory held the information throughout the entire exam period
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds information for only fractions of a second to a few seconds. The information was in LTM and needed a retrieval cue.

toLevel3.stem: If the right retrieval cue is not encountered, information stored in LTM may feel inaccessible even though it has not been permanently lost.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Retrieval requires appropriate cues. Without the right cue, stored information remains in LTM but cannot be brought into conscious awareness.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This is true. The absence of appropriate retrieval cues can make stored LTM information feel inaccessible without it being permanently lost.

toLevel3.stem: Retrieval explains how past {{blank:1}} becomes available for current use by bringing stored information from LTM into {{blank:2}} awareness in STM.
Some memories feel inaccessible because the right {{blank:1}} cue has not been encountered, even though the information remains {{blank:2}} in LTM.
Encoding transfers information from STM to LTM, while {{blank:1}} transfers information in the opposite direction, from {{blank:2}} back to STM.

toLevel4.stem: During a history exam, Liam cannot recall the date of an important event. Later, when he reads a newspaper article mentioning the same event, the date immediately comes to mind. Which explanation best applies the concept of retrieval?

options.text: The newspaper article provided a retrieval cue that activated the date stored in LTM, bringing it into STM
options.explanation: The article served as a retrieval cue that activated the stored date in LTM, bringing it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: The date was not in Liam's LTM and the newspaper article taught him the date for the first time
options.explanation: Liam had studied the date, so it was in LTM. The article triggered retrieval, not new encoding.

options.text: The newspaper article increased Liam's STM capacity, allowing the date to fit into conscious awareness
options.explanation: The article did not change STM capacity. It provided a retrieval cue that activated the stored information in LTM.

options.text: The date was permanently lost from LTM during the exam and recreated from the newspaper content
options.explanation: The date was in LTM but inaccessible during the exam. The article provided the retrieval cue needed to access it.

toLevel4.stem: A teacher plays a familiar song at the start of a revision lesson. Several students report that hearing the song brought back detailed memories of when they first learned the topic. Which aspect of retrieval does this scenario best demonstrate?

options.text: The song acted as a retrieval cue, activating associated information stored in LTM
options.explanation: The song served as a retrieval cue that activated memories associated with the original learning context, bringing them from LTM into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: The song replaced the students' existing memories with new information about the topic
options.explanation: The song did not replace memories. It activated existing memories stored in LTM through the retrieval process.

options.text: The song increased the duration of sensory memory so that old impressions became available again
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds information for only seconds. The song triggered retrieval from LTM, not an extension of sensory memory.

options.text: The song permanently transferred all of the students' LTM content into their STM simultaneously
options.explanation: Retrieval is selective and cue-dependent. The song activated specific associated memories, not all LTM content.

toLevel4.stem: Zara is trying to remember the name of a childhood friend. She cannot recall it until she looks at an old school photograph, at which point the name comes to her instantly. Which explanation is most consistent with the retrieval process?

options.text: The photograph provided a retrieval cue that activated the friend's name stored in LTM
options.explanation: The photograph acted as a retrieval cue, activating the name stored in LTM and bringing it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: The name was stored in sensory memory and the photograph extended its duration beyond normal limits
options.explanation: A childhood friend's name would be in LTM, not sensory memory. The photograph provided a retrieval cue for LTM.

options.text: The photograph displaced the name from STM into LTM, making it consciously accessible for the first time
options.explanation: The name was already in LTM. The photograph triggered its retrieval back into STM, not its initial storage.

options.text: The name was permanently deleted from memory and the photograph created an entirely new memory
options.explanation: The name was stored in LTM but inaccessible without the right cue. The photograph triggered retrieval, not new encoding.

toLevel4.stem: A study technique involves students writing exam-style questions about their notes and practising answering them. Based on the concept of retrieval, why might this technique be effective?

options.text: Practising retrieval strengthens the connections between cues and stored information in LTM
options.explanation: Practising retrieval by answering questions strengthens the pathways between retrieval cues and stored information in LTM, making future retrieval more likely.

options.text: Writing questions permanently moves all information from LTM into STM where it is always accessible
options.explanation: Information cannot be permanently moved from LTM to STM. The technique strengthens retrieval pathways, not permanent STM storage.

options.text: The technique works by increasing the capacity of sensory memory to hold more examination content
options.explanation: The technique does not affect sensory memory capacity. It strengthens retrieval pathways between cues and LTM information.

options.text: Writing questions deletes unnecessary information from LTM to reduce interference with important material
options.explanation: The technique does not delete LTM information. It strengthens retrieval by practising the process of accessing stored information.

toLevel4.stem: During a conversation, Elise smells freshly baked bread and suddenly recalls a detailed memory of baking with her grandmother as a child. Which aspect of retrieval does this best illustrate?

options.text: The smell acted as a retrieval cue that activated a specific episodic memory stored in LTM
options.explanation: The smell of bread served as a retrieval cue, activating the specific episodic memory of baking with her grandmother from LTM into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: The smell created an entirely new false memory that Elise mistakenly believes is a real childhood event
options.explanation: The smell triggered retrieval of an existing memory, not creation of a false memory. Retrieval cues activate stored information in LTM.

options.text: The smell increased Elise's STM capacity, allowing her to hold the full childhood memory simultaneously
options.explanation: The smell did not change STM capacity. It served as a retrieval cue that activated the stored memory in LTM.

options.text: The smell permanently transferred the memory from sensory memory where it had been stored since childhood
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds information for only seconds. The childhood memory was stored in LTM and was retrieved by the smell cue.

toLevel4.stem: A psychology student creates flashcards with keywords on one side and detailed information on the other. When studying, seeing each keyword helps them recall the related information. Which memory process is occurring when the student sees a keyword and recalls the information?

options.text: Retrieval — the keyword acts as a cue that activates stored information in LTM
options.explanation: The keyword on the flashcard acts as a retrieval cue, activating the related information stored in LTM and bringing it into conscious awareness in STM.

options.text: Encoding — the keyword is being transferred from sensory memory into STM for the first time
options.explanation: The student already knows the information. Seeing the keyword triggers retrieval from LTM, not initial encoding from sensory memory.

options.text: Storage — the keyword is being placed into LTM alongside the detailed information for later access
options.explanation: Storage has already occurred. When the student sees the keyword and recalls information, the process occurring is retrieval.

options.text: Displacement — the keyword pushes other information out of STM to make room for the recalled content
options.explanation: While STM has limited capacity, the primary process occurring is retrieval — the keyword cue activates stored LTM information.

toLevel4.stem: Two students study the same material. Student A reviews notes passively. Student B practises recalling information without looking at notes. On a test, Student B performs significantly better. Which explanation best applies the concept of retrieval?

options.text: Student B practised the retrieval process itself, strengthening the ability to access LTM information via cues
options.explanation: By practising retrieval, Student B strengthened the connections between retrieval cues and stored information in LTM, making recall on the test more effective.

options.text: Student B stored more information in sensory memory, which has unlimited capacity and permanent duration
options.explanation: Sensory memory does not have permanent duration. Student B's advantage came from practising the retrieval process, not from sensory memory.

options.text: Student A's passive review was equally effective but Student B was simply luckier on the test questions
options.explanation: Research supports that practising retrieval is more effective than passive review. The difference is not due to luck.

options.text: Student B displaced all unnecessary information from STM, creating more room for new exam answers
options.explanation: The advantage was not about STM space. Student B strengthened retrieval pathways by practising accessing information from LTM.

toLevel4.stem: When Liam read a newspaper article about the event, it acted as a {{blank:1}} cue that activated the date stored in {{blank:2}}, bringing it into conscious awareness.
Practising answering exam-style questions strengthens the connections between {{blank:1}} cues and stored information, making future {{blank:2}} from LTM more likely.
When Elise smelled freshly baked bread, the scent acted as a retrieval cue that activated an {{blank:1}} memory of baking with her grandmother, bringing it from LTM into {{blank:2}}.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher finds that participants recall more words from a list when tested in the same room where they learned the words, compared to a different room. Which analysis of this finding best relates to the concept of retrieval cues?

options.text: The original room provided contextual retrieval cues that were encoded alongside the words, facilitating retrieval from LTM
options.explanation: Environmental context is encoded alongside target information. Being in the same room provides contextual retrieval cues that activate the stored words in LTM.

options.text: The original room increased the capacity of STM, allowing more words to be held simultaneously during the test
options.explanation: The room did not change STM capacity. It provided contextual retrieval cues that facilitated access to information stored in LTM.

options.text: The different room permanently deleted the words from LTM, making them impossible to retrieve under any conditions
options.explanation: A different room does not delete information from LTM. The words were less accessible because the retrieval cues from the original context were absent.

options.text: The original room stored the words in sensory memory, which preserved them until the test was administered
options.explanation: Sensory memory holds information for only seconds. The words were stored in LTM and retrieved more easily with matching contextual cues.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'If I cannot recall something, it means the information was never properly stored in LTM in the first place.' Which evaluation of this claim is most accurate?

options.text: Incorrect — the information may be stored but inaccessible because the right retrieval cue has not been encountered
options.explanation: Failure to recall does not necessarily mean the information was not stored. It may be in LTM but inaccessible because the appropriate retrieval cue has not been encountered.

options.text: Entirely correct — any information that cannot be recalled has definitely not been stored in LTM at all
options.explanation: This is too absolute. Information can be stored in LTM but remain inaccessible without the right retrieval cue, as demonstrated by the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon.

options.text: Incorrect — all information is always retrievable from LTM regardless of whether cues are present or not
options.explanation: Not all stored information is always retrievable. Retrieval depends on appropriate cues. The student's error is assuming failure means no storage, not that all LTM is always accessible.

options.text: Entirely correct — LTM has unlimited retrieval so any stored information can always be accessed instantly
options.explanation: LTM does not have unlimited retrieval. Information in LTM requires retrieval cues to be brought into conscious awareness in STM.

toLevel5.stem: The 'tip-of-the-tongue' phenomenon occurs when a person feels certain they know a word but cannot quite retrieve it. Which analysis best explains this phenomenon using the concept of retrieval?

options.text: The information is stored in LTM but the available retrieval cues are insufficient to fully activate it
options.explanation: The tip-of-the-tongue state shows that information is stored in LTM (the person feels they know it) but the current retrieval cues are not sufficient to fully activate and bring it into STM.

options.text: The information has been permanently deleted from LTM and the feeling of knowing is a false sensation
options.explanation: The feeling of knowing typically reflects that the information is stored. It is the retrieval process that is partially failing due to insufficient cues.

options.text: The information is in sensory memory but has not yet been transferred to STM for conscious processing
options.explanation: Previously learned words are stored in LTM, not sensory memory. The issue is incomplete retrieval from LTM due to insufficient cues.

options.text: The information was never encoded because the person only has a vague feeling with no actual stored memory
options.explanation: The strong feeling of knowing and ability to recall partial information suggest the word is stored. The issue is insufficient retrieval cues.

toLevel5.stem: A teacher argues that multiple-choice tests are easier than essay tests because they provide retrieval cues. Which evaluation of this argument is most accurate?

options.text: Valid — multiple-choice options act as recognition cues that aid retrieval, while essays require self-generated cues for recall
options.explanation: Multiple-choice options provide external cues (recognition), whereas essay questions require the student to generate their own retrieval cues (recall), making essays more demanding on the retrieval process.

options.text: Invalid — both test formats require identical retrieval processes with no differences in cue availability
options.explanation: The two formats differ in retrieval demands. Multiple-choice provides recognition cues; essays require self-generated retrieval cues.

options.text: Valid — but only because multiple-choice tests bypass LTM entirely and test sensory memory instead
options.explanation: Multiple-choice tests do not bypass LTM. They provide external retrieval cues that facilitate access to LTM information.

options.text: Invalid — essay tests are actually easier because writing activates procedural memory which aids all recall
options.explanation: The motor act of writing does not aid retrieval from LTM. The key difference is that essays require self-generated retrieval cues while multiple-choice provides them.

toLevel5.stem: Research on retrieval practice shows that actively recalling information strengthens memory more than passively re-reading the same material. Which analysis best explains this finding?

options.text: Active retrieval strengthens the pathways between cues and stored LTM information, making future retrieval more efficient
options.explanation: Each successful retrieval strengthens the connection between the cue and the stored information in LTM, making the retrieval pathway more efficient for future use.

options.text: Active retrieval deletes weak memories from LTM, leaving only the strongest memories which are easier to access
options.explanation: Retrieval practice does not delete memories. It strengthens the pathways between retrieval cues and stored information.

options.text: Passive re-reading is actually more effective but researchers have not yet been able to measure its true benefits
options.explanation: Research consistently shows retrieval practice is more effective. The benefit comes from strengthening retrieval pathways.

options.text: Active retrieval works by increasing the biological capacity of STM so more information can be held at once
options.explanation: Retrieval practice does not increase STM capacity. It strengthens the connections between cues and stored LTM information.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Retrieval cues are unnecessary because once information is in LTM, it should be automatically available whenever needed.' Which evaluation is most accurate?

options.text: Incorrect — LTM requires cues to bring information into conscious awareness; without cues, stored information may remain inaccessible
options.explanation: Retrieval is not automatic. Information in LTM requires appropriate retrieval cues to be brought into conscious awareness in STM. Without cues, stored information can feel inaccessible.

options.text: Entirely correct — all information in LTM is always automatically and instantly available for conscious use
options.explanation: LTM information is not automatically available. The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon and context-dependent memory demonstrate that retrieval cues are needed.

options.text: Incorrect — but only because LTM does not actually exist as a separate store in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model
options.explanation: LTM does exist as a distinct store in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model. The student's error is assuming that stored information is automatically accessible without cues.

options.text: Entirely correct — retrieval cues are only needed for sensory memory, not for information stored in LTM
options.explanation: Retrieval cues are needed to access LTM information. Sensory memory does not use retrieval cues in the same way; its information fades automatically.

toLevel5.stem: A study finds that emotional state can act as a retrieval cue: participants who learned material while happy recalled more when tested in a happy state. Which analysis of this finding is most consistent with the concept of retrieval?

options.text: Emotional state was encoded alongside the material, and matching the state during testing provided an effective retrieval cue
options.explanation: Emotional state is encoded as part of the context during learning. When the same emotional state is present during testing, it acts as a retrieval cue that facilitates access to the stored information.

options.text: Happy participants had larger STM capacity, allowing them to hold more information during the test
options.explanation: Emotional state does not change STM capacity. The matching emotional state served as a retrieval cue for information stored in LTM.

options.text: Emotional state permanently altered the information stored in LTM, making it only accessible in that state
options.explanation: Emotional state does not permanently alter LTM content. It is encoded as context that can serve as a retrieval cue, but information may be accessible through other cues as well.

options.text: The finding is irrelevant to retrieval because emotions are processed by the amygdala which is not part of the memory system
options.explanation: The amygdala is part of the memory system. The finding demonstrates that emotional state can function as a retrieval cue within the retrieval process.

toLevel5.stem: A textbook states: 'Retrieval failure is the only possible explanation for forgetting.' Which evaluation of this claim is most justified?

options.text: Too narrow — forgetting can also result from encoding failure, decay, displacement, or interference, not just retrieval failure
options.explanation: Retrieval failure is one explanation for forgetting, but information can also be lost through poor encoding, decay in STM, displacement, or interference. The claim is too narrow.

options.text: Entirely correct — all forgetting is caused by retrieval failure because all information is permanently stored in LTM
options.explanation: Not all information reaches LTM. Forgetting can occur at any stage of the memory system, not only through retrieval failure.

options.text: Entirely incorrect — retrieval failure never contributes to forgetting because LTM has automatic and unlimited access
options.explanation: Retrieval failure is a genuine cause of forgetting. The claim is too narrow, not entirely wrong.

options.text: Correct for STM but incorrect for LTM because STM has unlimited duration preventing any forgetting
options.explanation: STM has limited duration (18–30 seconds), not unlimited. The claim is too narrow because forgetting has multiple causes across all stores.

toLevel5.stem: Context-dependent memory research shows that environmental cues present during {{blank:1}} can serve as retrieval cues during {{blank:2}}, improving recall when contexts match.
The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon demonstrates that information can be {{blank:1}} in LTM but remain temporarily {{blank:2}} due to insufficient retrieval cues.
